Resource Report 1 – General Description


Request 1.     Section 1.2.1.1 states that the Joliet Loop and Sycamore Loop would be
               “constructed 50 feet offset from Guardian’s existing pipeline and within adjacent
               easements…each new loop pipeline will be centered within a 50-foot-wide
               permanent easement abutting Guardian’s existing easement, creating a
               combined permanent right-of-way that is generally 100 feet in width.” Justify
               the need for a 100-foot-wide permanent right-of-way, including why a 50-foot
               setback of the pipeline loops from existing lines would be required. Note that the
               typical width of a permanent easement for two collocated pipelines owned by the
               same operator is 75 feet.

Response:

Guardian proposes a combined 100-foot wide permanent right-of-way (50-foot existing and 50-foot
new) with a 50-foot offset between pipelines for the Joliet Loop and Sycamore Loop in accordance
with the permanent right-of-way widths and offsets for 36-inch, co-located pipelines recommended
by the Interstate Natural Gas Association of America ("INGAA") referenced in "Building Interstate
Natural Gas Transmission Pipelines: A Primer (INGAA, 2013)". The proposed permanent right-of-
way width and offset will improve worker and pipeline safety during any future integrity management
excavation or class change replacement construction activities by adhering to recommended industry-
wide safety practice to avoid operating construction equipment over or adjacent to existing in-service
pipelines.

Request 3.     Section 1.3.1.7 states “Vegetation removed during clearing will be redistributed
               across the right-of-way” and “Construction debris and surplus material will be
               removed unless otherwise approved by the landowner or land-managing
               agency.” The FERC Upland Erosion Control, Revegetation, and Maintenance
               Plan (Plan) at sections III.E and V.A.6 requires the “regular collection,
               containment, and disposal” of construction debris except as used “for beneficial
               reuse, stabilization, or habitat restoration.” Further clarify how Guardian would
               dispose of vegetation removed during clearing and “construction debris and
               surplus material” and how the proposed measures would be consistent with the
               FERC Plan at sections III.E and V.A.6.

Response:
Herbaceous vegetation within the construction right-of-way will be removed and/or displaced during
the course of construction through grading, trench excavation, and equipment travel, and will be
naturally redistributed across the right-of-way during re-grading and restoration. Woody vegetation
(e.g., brush, shrubs, trees) will be managed in one of the following ways:

   •   stockpiled at an accessible location at the edge of the construction right of-way or adjacent to
       it, but not within 50 feet of any wetland or waterbody, for beneficial reuse by the landowner;
   •   chipped and stockpiled at the edge of the construction right-of-way or adjacent to it, but not
       within 50 feet of any wetland or waterbody, for beneficial reuse by the landowner;
   •   chipped and spread across the right-of-way (within non-agricultural upland areas only); or
   •   hauled to an approved disposal facility.

Construction debris and surplus material include excess woody material and excess rock. These
materials will either be stockpiled at the edge of the construction right-of-way or adjacent to it, but
not within 50 feet of any wetland or waterbody, for beneficial reuse by the landowner or hauled to an
approved disposal facility. If a landowner requests to retain surplus materials, Guardian will obtain a
written agreement from the landowner confirming their intent to beneficially reuse the materials.
Guardian will retain the right to remove and dispose of the materials if they are not retrieved by the
landowner within the agreed upon timeframe.

Request 8.    Section 2.1.5 states “During field surveys, seeps or springs were identified within
              150 feet of the Project area and captured in the Wetland and Waterbody
              Delineation Report (See Appendix 2C).” However, Guardian’s Wetland and
              Waterbody Delineation Report does not appear to identify seeps or springs
              within the environmental survey corridor. Therefore:

              a. identify all seeps and springs within 150 feet of all Project workspaces, by
                 milepost, and indicate where these features are indicative of karst formation;
              b. describe how Guardian would protect any springs within and immediately
                 adjacent to Project workspace from physical damage or destruction; and
              c. identify any springs that are used as a potable water supply.

Response:
   a. To date, no seeps or springs, including those used as a potable water supply, have been identified
      within 150 feet of Project workspaces based on landowner communications and field surveys
      conducted in Fall 2025 and Spring 2026. However, biological field surveys are still in progress
      with the remaining tracts anticipated to be surveyed in Fall 2026 where landowner approval is
      granted. The results of those surveys will be included in the supplemental filing planned for
      November 2026.
   b. If a seep/spring is identified within Project workspaces, Guardian will install and work off of
      timber mats over the seep/spring. If a seep/spring is identified within 150 feet of Project
      workspaces, Guardian will install signage at the edge of the construction right-of-way adjacent to
      the seep/spring and maintain appropriate sediment and erosion control devices to prevent silt laden
      water from flowing off the right-of-way and into the adjacent feature. All equipment would be
      parked and/or fueled at least 100 feet away from the seep/spring and no hazardous materials would
      be stored within 100 feet of the seep/spring in accordance with the FERC’s Wetland and
      Waterbody Construction and Mitigation Procedures ("Procedures") and Guardian’s Spill
      Prevention, Control, and Countermeasures Plan.
   c. See response 8(a).

Request 9.           Clarify the remediation status (e.g., open, closed, closed with controls) for the
                     Ranger Enterprises Inc. leaking underground storage tank site identified 168
                     feet from Project workspace.

Response:

A review of publicly available records from the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency (“IEPA”)
and the Illinois Office of the State Fire Marshal (“OSFM”) indicates that the Ranger Enterprises
Inc. leaking underground storage tank (“LUST”) site (Incident No. 951963; LPC No. 0370055010),
located at 13845 State Route 38, Cortland, Illinois, is a closed release site 1. The release was reported
to the Illinois Emergency Management Agency (“IEMA”) on September 20, 1995. IEPA records
indicate that a Notice of Release Letter was issued on September 25, 1995, a Professional Engineer
Certification was received on December 20, 1995, a Corrective Action Completion Report was
submitted on April 18, 1996, and a No Further Remediation (“NFR”) determination was issued on
April 19, 1996. Issuance of the NFR letter indicates that corrective action requirements associated
with the release were completed and no further remediation was required by the agency.
Furthermore, A review of OSFM underground storage tank records further indicates that the facility
is classified as Exempt and that three gasoline underground storage tanks (560-gallon, 560-gallon,
and 1,000-gallon) were removed on September 27, 1995 2. The OSFM database does not identify
any active underground storage tanks, active permits, current deficiencies, or associated release
numbers for the facility. In addition, the IEPA database does not identify any institutional controls,
environmental land use controls (“ELUCs”), groundwater use restrictions, engineered barriers,
worker caution requirements, or soil handling restrictions associated with the site. Based on the
records reviewed, the Ranger Enterprises Inc. LUST site appears to be closed without controls.

Request 14. Clarify what BMPs would be in place regarding the three waterbodies that are listed
            as impaired, as outlined in Table 2.2.5-1 in the application.

Response:
Aux Sable Creek and Coon Creek will be crossed via conventional bore. This trenchless crossing method
will avoid in-water work and loss of vegetation cover, minimizing the risk of Project activities contributing
to impairment of these waterbodies. Guardian will install sediment and erosion controls around
workspaces upgradient of the waterbodies to prevent silt-laden water carrying potential pollutants from
entering the waterbodies. Guardian will also implement its Spill Prevention Control and Countermeasures
(“SPCC”) Plan to minimize the risk of hazardous materials entering the waterbodies. Lawrence Creek will
be crossed via an open cut dry crossing method (i.e., dam-and-pump or flume). The pollutants responsible
for aquatic life impairment in Lawrence Creek are unknown. As such, Guardian cannot develop pollutant-
specific best management practices ("BMPs"). However, the use of dry crossing methods will minimize
downstream turbidity and sedimentation that could contribute to reduced levels of dissolved oxygen. In
addition, instream construction activities will be completed within 24 hours consistent with the FERC’s
Procedures to minimize disturbances to aquatic life. Appropriate erosion and sediment control devices
will be installed upgradient of the waterbody and preventative plans will be implemented as described for
Aux Sable Creek and Coon Creek. Lawrence Creek will be restored to preconstruction contours and
conditions and stabilized using appropriate measures such as seeding, planting, erosion control blankets,
or riprap, as site conditions warrant to prevent stream bank erosion and degradation of habitat for aquatic
life.

Request 16. Confirm the source for hydrostatic testing water and the method of transportation to
            the Project location. Also clarify if the hydrostatic test water discharge location has
            been identified.

Response:

Based on the Project design, hydrostatic test water will either be discharged on-site in accordance with
the Illinois and Wisconsin hydrostatic test discharge permits (see Revised Table 1.9-1 in EIR 6 response)
or hauled off to an approved disposal facility. Guardian will obtain test water from municipal sources,
either by piping it directly to the site or transporting it by truck. Water from hydrostatic testing will only

Response:

Guardian will install sectionalizing block valves with remote valve actuation for rupture mitigation shut-
off of the four (4) mainline pipeline segments spaced in accordance with the requirements of 192.179.

Guardian will also use a Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition system across its pipeline network.
This system continuously tracks key metrics such as gas pressure, temperature, and volume at designated
points along the pipeline. Real-time data is delivered to operators through this system along with an alarm
to alert operators if critical parameters exceed set thresholds. Guardian personnel will continuously
monitor this system from its central gas control center.

The compressor Stations (Eden and Joliet) will install pressure limiting devices per §192.171, an
emergency shutdown system per §192.167, and gas detection in the compressor building per §192.736.
All pressure relieving devices shall be designed to meet the capacity requirements of §192.743 and
inspected and tested per §192.739.

2.2    PROJECT PURPOSE AND NEED

The purpose of the Project is to meet the growing demand for additional natural gas supplies in
Wisconsin and neighboring states by creating additional firm transportation capacity from liquid
trading hubs in the Chicago area to points of delivery in Wisconsin. Specifically, as evidenced by
binding precedent agreements with the Project Shippers, the Project responds directly to
increasing natural gas demand required to satisfy growing local distribution company (LDC)
demand (principally critical winter load), maintain electric grid reliability, meet growing electricity
generation requirements arising from increased power demand and from retirement of coal-fired
generation. The Project Shippers and the upper Midwest region generally will benefit from the
Project because the additional capacity will help meet growing regional energy demands from
diverse supplies, in turn helping to maintain affordable energy costs in the region.

The Project is strategically positioned to meet this significant market demand by providing Project
Shippers with access to abundant domestic and Canadian natural gas supplies at the Chicago
trading hubs, such as the Guardian Hub, the ANR-Joliet Hub, and the Alliance Chicago Exchange,
where such hubs receive natural gas from diverse sources, such as the Permian Basin, the
Rockies, the Bakken, the Gulf Coast, Appalachia, Western Canada Sedimentary Basin, and other
supply basins. The Project’s additional capacity, created primarily through looping existing
pipeline segments and adding compression, will be able to transport these diverse supplies to
demand centers to meet the increasing need for natural gas deliveries in Wisconsin and other
neighboring Midwest states.

The Project has strong market support, evidenced by executed binding precedent agreements for
approximately 536,903 Dth/day of long-term firm transportation capacity. The precedent
agreements represent 100 percent of the Project’s firm transportation capacity, demonstrating
unambiguous support for the Project and its importance for meeting energy requirements of
Wisconsin and Iowa. The Project Shippers’ commitments to the Project are corroborated by the
independent analysis prepared by Brown Williams, Moorhead, and Quinn, Inc. (G3 Market Study).
This G3 Market Study demonstrates that the demand for natural gas is increasing in Wisconsin
and neighboring states due to increasing demand of natural gas commercial and residential end-
users and due to power generation demand resulting from both the increase in commercial and
residential power demand and the retirement of coal-fired generation..

typically progress like an assembly line, with construction crews advancing along the right-of-way

restoration—may extend for approximately four to five months or longer.

Sections of pipe (a.k.a. “joints”), typically 40 to 80 feet in length, will be delivered to the right-of-

protective coating to limit contact with moisture (e.g., fusion-bonded epoxy, abrasion-resistant

hydraulic bending machine. The joints will then be aligned, welded into continuous segments, and
placed on temporary supports along the trench edge. Welding will be performed by qualified
personnel in accordance with 49 CFR 192 Subpart E, American Petroleum Institute
Standard 1104, and other applicable requirements. Weld integrity will be verified through non-
destructive testing methods, such as radiographic or ultrasonic inspection, to identify and repair
any defects prior to lowering the pipe into the trench. Tie-in crews will circle back to complete
connections at specific locations, including waterbody and road crossings, MLV sites, and points
where new loop pipelines connect to existing lines.

3.4.15 Horizontal Directional Drill

Horizontal directional drill (HDD) is a trenchless construction technique that involves boring under
a ground surface feature (e.g., waterbodies or other sensitive resources) and installing a
prefabricated pipeline segment through the drilled path. This method eliminates surface
disturbance between the drill entry and exit points and is often selected for areas where
conventional installation would pose environmental or engineering challenges. HDDs offer
advantages such as minimizing riparian tree clearing, avoiding in-stream work, and reducing
overall surface impacts.

Although HDDs offer notable advantages in the avoidance of ground surface features, they also
have limitations that must be considered when evaluating the feasibility of utilizing this
construction technique. Site conditions, soil formations, terrain, existing utilities, and workspace
constraints all contribute to evaluating the feasibility of an HDD. Any one of these considerations
can significantly impact the viability of a potential HDD. For example, workspace requirements at
the entry and exit locations of the HDD are significant and usually much greater than the limit of
disturbance width for standard, open-cut pipeline construction. HDD feasibility is also highly
dependent on geotechnical conditions as subsurface conditions largely determine the profile
geometry of an HDD and thus the constructability to avoid a particular ground surface feature.

Guardian will employ a steering coil system for the Highway 34 HDD and a gyroscopic steering
system for the West Aux Sable Creek and Little Rock Creek HDDs to maintain alignment along
the pipeline centerline and minimize vegetation clearing. A Magnetic Wireline Tracking System
(steering coil) is used where surface access is impractical or physically impossible, drill depth
exceeds walkover capabilities, or signal interference is significant. This system transmits data
using a wireline connection from a probe in the bottom-hole assembly to the operator via a
magnetic field. Alternatively, gyroscopic systems control the drill head’s orientation and trajectory
by sensing angular motion and the Earth’s rotation. A guidance wire is placed along the drill path
to transmit data from the drill bit to the surface for real-time monitoring but is not used to generate
a reference field.

The HDD process begins with positioning a drill rig at the entry point and drilling a small-diameter
pilot hole along a predetermined path beneath the feature using a powered drill bit. As the drill
advances, additional drill pipe segments are added to extend the bore. The drill bit is continuously
monitored and steered to maintain the desired alignment. Once the pilot hole is complete, the
electric sensor grid is removed.

may not be visible if it does not eventually connect to a vertical path that extends to the surface.
The extent of inadvertent return can vary depending on the size of the pathway, the permeability
of the geologic material, the viscosity of the fluid, and the pressure of the hydraulic drilling system.
Conditions such as unconsolidated gravel, coarse sand, or fractured bedrock increase risk of one
of these events. Guardian will continuously monitor HDD activities for inadvertent releases by
visually inspecting the features being crossed. A 10-foot-wide path in the vegetation between
entry and exit points may be cleared using hand tools to promote visibility and aid in monitoring.

were to occur. If a release occurs in uplands or wetlands, containment pits will first be excavated

waterbody releases, containment is more challenging due to dispersion. Mitigation strategies may
involve adding non-hazardous thickening agents to the drilling fluid, such as bentonite or
cottonseed hulls, to seal the flow path and prevent further release. All additives will be approved

3.4.16 Conventional Bore

Conventional boring is a trenchless installation method used to place short segments of
prefabricated pipeline beneath surface features such as roads or railways. This technique
involves excavating pits on either side of the crossing and boring a hole through the substrate
from one pit to the other. If water is present in the pits, Guardian will conduct dewatering in
accordance with applicable permits and in a manner that prevents erosion and avoids the
discharge of sediment-laden water into nearby wetlands and waterbodies.

Once the borehole is completed, a prefabricated segment of pipeline will be pulled through the
opening. For longer crossings, multiple pipe sections may be welded together into a continuous
string prior to installation. Conventional bores, similar to HDDs, minimize ground surface
disturbance; however, its use is limited in areas with saturated soils where maintaining borehole
stability is not feasible.

Although conventional bores offer notable advantages in the avoidance of ground surface
features, they also have limitations that must be considered when evaluating the feasibility of
utilizing this construction technique. Site conditions and access, terrain, existing utilities, and
workspace constraints all contribute to evaluating the feasibility of a conventional bore, and any
one of these considerations can significantly impact the viability of a conventional bore. For
example, conventional bores have limited constructable crossing length and bore pits for a
conventional bore have a limited constructable set-up depth without significant safety design
considerations. These considerations can limit the feasibility of crossing beneath a particular
ground surface feature with sufficient separation depth.

To reduce the risk of fuel, lubricant, or chemical spills near waterbodies, Guardian will prohibit
refueling, overnight parking, and concrete coating activities within 100 feet of a waterbody unless
the EI determines no reasonable alternative exists and appropriate spill prevention and
containment measures are implemented. If refueling within 100 feet of a waterbody is necessary,
Guardian will follow its Spill Prevention, Control, and Countermeasure Plan (SPCC Plan) (see

that Guardian will take with respect to fuels, hazardous materials, and other controlled

These construction procedures have been designed to minimize impacts to waterbodies. To
further reduce the duration of in-stream work, Guardian will prepare the work area on both sides
of the crossing prior to trenching.

Dam-and-Pump Crossing Method

The dam-and-pump technique uses temporary dams, typically constructed of sandbags and
plastic sheeting, which are installed upstream and downstream of the waterbody crossing
location. Once the dams are in place, the stream flow is diverted around the construction

Flume Crossing Method

The flume crossing technique uses one or more flume pipes to temporarily direct streamflow over
the crossing location. This approach allows trenching and pipeline installation to occur beneath
the flumes while maintaining stream flow. To direct water into the flumes, two bulkheads (e.g.,
sandbags or plastic sheeting) will be installed upstream and downstream of the crossing. The
bulkheads and flume pipes will be removed following pipeline installation, trench backfill, and
streambank restoration. This method is favorable because it reduces downstream turbidity by
enabling excavation under relatively dry conditions.

materials, and other controlled substances.

upland areas and filtered through dewatering structures to slow the discharge rate and minimize
erosion. Discharge of heavily silt-laden water into wetlands will not be permitted.
